newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian PM Dehaene seen hard to replace.
newsitem.headline: Belgian PM Dehaene seen hard to replace.

text.p: Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, master dealmaker of Belgian politics and widely seen as one of few people able to hold the country together, has said he will not stand for a third term in elections due in 1999.

"After two mandates, one has probably given the best one has. In one's own interest, it is best to stop then. Next time I will pass on the baton, if it is up to me," he told the daily newspaper De Standaard.
The decision may expose Belgium's political system -- already damaged by revelations in the double child sex and political murder scandals -- to a bruising fight for the succession.
Dehaene -- a 56-year-old Christian Democrat from Flanders, the Dutch-speaking northern half of the country -- has been a key figure in Belgian politics since the early 1980s.
He became prime minister of a centre-left government in March 1992 and started a second term in June 1995.
"Dehaene has been one of the exceptional elements in keeping north and south together. He would be very hard to replace," said Lieven De Winter, a political analyst at UCL university.

The 1999 elections, though still far away, are expected to be difficult. Flemish politicians have stressed again and again that the next government must make progress in making Belgium a more federal state, while Wallonia tries to block this.
Many analysts also expect that the next government will be a centre-right coalition between the Christian Democrats and the conservative liberal parties.
"On average, the Christian Democrats switch coalition partners about every six years," De Winter said.
Dehaene rose to power through the ranks of the Christian Democratic labour movement ACW, and is not seen as an ideal candidate to head a government with the liberals.
The succession is seen as difficult, because he is one of the few Flemish politicians with enough credibility on the other side of the language divide.
A new prime minister is most likely to come from Dehaene's party, the CVP, which is the main party in Flanders which has six million of the country's 10 million inhabitants.
Among CVP politicians, Budget Minister Herman van Rompuy, a close friend of Dehaene, is seen as the leading contender.
Van Rompuy is closer to the more conservative forces in the CVP, and therefore more likely to lead a centre-right cabinet.

Like Dehaene, Van Rompuy is fairly acceptable to the francophone half of the country. But Van Rompuy is an intellectual, somewhat quiet figure, in sharp contrast to the charismatic, political brawler Dehaene.
Van Rompuy also lacks Dehaene's intimate knowledge of Belgium's federal and regional state system, a system so complex that most Belgians fail to understand it.
Another possibility is that Wallonia, the francophone half of Belgium, would provide the prime minister, an honour it has not had since 1974.
Dehaene's surprise announcement that he would not seek reelection is seen as partly motivated by his ambitions to succeed to European Commission President Jacques Santer.
In 1994, Dehaene narrowly lost a bid to become president of the European Commission because of a veto by British Prime Minister John Major, who considered him too pro-European.
Asked whether he still hoped to get the highest EU post when Santer's mandate ends in 1999, Dehaene told De Standaard: "A chance like that you only get once in a lifetime."
But in an interview with daily La Libre Belgique Dehaene said that the coming years were crucial for Europe, with the single currency and the expansion towards eastern Europe ahead.
"These are the main challenges for Europe and I count on working hard on these, even if (the opposition) will say I am working for my own career."
